Relative monadicity
Nathanael Arkor, Dylan McDermott

Abstract
. We establish a relative monadicity theorem for relative monads with dense roots in a virtual equipment, specialising to a relative monadicity theorem for enriched relative monads. In particular, for a dense 𝕍 {\mathbb{V}} -functor j : A → E j\colon A\to E , a 𝕍 {\mathbb{V}} -functor r : D → E r\colon D\to E is j j -monadic if and only if r r admits a left j j -relative adjoint and creates j j -absolute colimits. This provides a refinement of the classical monadicity theorem – characterising those categories whose objects are given by those of E E equipped with algebraic structure – in which the arities of the algebraic operations are valued in A A . In particular, when j = 1 j=1 , we recover a formal monadicity theorem. Furthermore, we examine the interaction between the pasting law for relative adjunctions and relative monadicity. As a consequence, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the ( j j -relative) monadicity of the composite of a 𝕍 {\mathbb{V}} -functor with a ( j j -relatively) monadic 𝕍 {\mathbb{V}} -functor.



2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
18D70,18D65,18C15,18C20,18A40,18C10,18D20,18N10

1.
Introduction

The concept of
monadicity
is fundamental in category theory. A functor
r\colon D\to E
is said to be monadic if it exhibits
D
as the category of algebras for a monad on
E
. Conceptually, this permits the identification of the objects of
D
with objects of
E
equipped with algebraic structure – often expressible concretely in terms of operations and equations – and the morphisms of
D
as morphisms of
E
that preserve the algebraic structure. Having such a description of
D
is useful as it facilitates the application of monad theory, for instance in providing techniques to lift structure from
E
to
D
.

Given that we are interested in the monadicity of functors, it is important to have methods for establishing monadicity. A
monadicity theorem
provides sufficient (and often also necessary) conditions for a functor to be monadic
[
Bec66
,
Par71
]
. Monadicity theorems are particularly convenient tools in two kinds of situations. First, in concrete examples, it can be simpler to verify a set of monadicity conditions for
r
than to directly construct an equivalence between
D
and the category of algebras for an induced monad, particularly when the categories in question are complex. Second, in abstract examples, there may not be an amenable description of the category of algebras for the induced monad. This is typically the case, for example, when the existence of a left adjoint to
r
has been deduced abstractly via an adjoint functor theorem, rather than by giving a concrete description of the left adjoint.

In many situations we are concerned not only with whether the objects of
D
may be identified with objects of
E
equipped with algebraic structure, but also with the nature of that algebraic structure. An algebra for a monad may be viewed as an object equipped with operations of arbitrary arity, along with equations imposing laws that the operations must satisfy. In practice, we frequently wish to restrict attention not to arbitrary algebras, but only to those that may be axiomatised in terms of operations with particular arity. For instance, in universal algebra, it is typical to consider specifically those algebras that admit a description in terms of finitary operations
[
Bir35
]
. From a concrete perspective, this can be desirable because such algebras admit a tractable syntactic description; from an abstract perspective, categories of such algebras typically have stronger categorical properties. In these situations, the classical notion of monadicity proves too coarse, as monads make no distinction between the possible arities of operations for algebras and the possible carriers for algebras.

A
relative monad
is a refinement of the notion of monad that relaxes the requirement that the monad’s underlying functor be an endofunctor
[
ACU10
,
ACU15
]
. A monad relative to a functor
j\colon A\to E
may be viewed as a generalisation of the notion of monad in which the possible arities of operations for algebras are valued in
A
, while the possible carriers for algebras are valued in
E
. Just as for ordinary monads, every
j
-relative monad has a category of algebras, equipped with free and forgetful functors
f_{T}\colon A\to\mathbf{Alg}(T)
and
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E
that together form a
j
-relative adjunction
f_{T}\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}u_{T}
, i.e. a family of bijections
\mathbf{Alg}(T)(f_{T}x,y)\cong E(jx,u_{T}y)
natural in
x
and
y

[
ACU15
,
Ulm68
]
.

A functor
r\colon D\to E
is said to be
j
-relatively monadic
(or simply
j
-monadic
) if it exhibits
D
as the category of algebras for a
j
-relative monad. Conceptually, this permits the identification of the objects of
D
with objects of
E
equipped with algebraic structure whose arities are valued, via
j
, in the category
A
. For instance, if
j\colon A\to E
is the inclusion of a full subcategory of finite objects, a
j
-monadic functor
r
exhibits
D
as a category of algebras whose operations are finitary. Relative monadicity thus provides the sought-after refinement of monadicity; it is indeed a refinement since, when
j
is the identity functor on
E
, relative monadicity is simply ordinary monadicity. It is consequently desirable to establish
relative monadicity theorems
, extending the classical monadicity theorems. This is the motivation for the present paper.

In this paper, we establish two relative monadicity theorems. The first (
Theorem

4.7
) is a characterisation in the style of
[
Bec66
]
and
[
Par71
]
, establishing that, for
r
to be
j
-monadic, it is necessary and sufficient that
r
admits a left
j
-relative adjoint and creates certain colimits. The second (
Theorem

6.5
) is a pasting law for relatively monadic functors, which may be seen as analogous to the pasting law for pullbacks, characterising the relative monadicity of one functor in terms of the relative monadicity of another.

1.1.
Relative monadicity via creation of colimits

For
j
the identity functor on a category
E
, a
j
-relative monad is a (non-relative) monad, and there is a well-known characterisation of
j
-monadicity: a functor
r\colon D\to E
is monadic if and only if it admits a left adjoint and creates coequalisers of
r
-contractible pairs
[
Bec66
]
; or, equivalently, if and only if it admits a left adjoint and creates absolute colimits
[
Par71
]
.

For more general functors
j
, there are also known characterisations of
j
-monadicity. However, perhaps surprisingly, these characterisations predate the modern notion of relative monad by some thirty-five years.
[
Die75
,
Die76
]
and
[
Lee77
]
independently established that a functor
r\colon D\to E
is monadic relative to a dense and fully faithful functor
j\colon A\to E
if and only if it admits a left
j
-relative adjoint and creates
j
-absolute colimits
1
1

1

A colimit in
E
is
j
-absolute
when it is preserved by the nerve functor
E(j{-}_{2},{-}_{1})\colon E\to[A{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]
.
. Due to the relative obscurity of the sources, and because the notions of relative monad studied by
[
Die75
]
and
[
Lee77
]
appear quite different to that of
[
ACU10
]
(cf.
[
AM24
, Example 8.14]
), these relative monadicity theorems have till now been overlooked.

While the characterisations of
[
Die75
]
and
[
Lee77
]
are useful, there are two respects in which one might hope for greater generality. First, we should like to drop the assumption that the root
j
be fully faithful. Second, we should like a similar characterisation in the setting of enriched category theory, extending that for enriched monadicity
[
Bun69
,
Dub70
]
.

The purpose of
Section

4
is to establish such a characterisation. However, our approach is more general still. It is the philosophy of formal category theory that the various flavours of category theory – such as ordinary category theory, enriched category theory, internal category theory, and so on – should all be viewed as instances of a general theory. That is, rather than establish the fundamental theorems of category theory separately in each setting, it is valuable to instead work in a framework in which such theorems may be proven just once, and then specialised to each setting. This was the approach of
[
AM24
]
, in which we laid the foundations for a formal theory of relative monads. Herein, we follow the same approach, working in the context of a virtual equipment in the sense of
[
CS10
]
. Thus, we shall first establish a relative monadicity theorem in the context of a virtual equipment, from which an enriched relative monadicity theorem will follow as a special case (cf.
[
AM24
, §8]
). However, we are able to make some simplifications for enrichment in well-behaved monoidal categories, which we describe in
Section

5
.

1.2.
Relative monadicity via composition

Given a monadic functor
r^{\prime}\colon D\to E
, it is often useful to establish when precomposing some functor
r\colon C\to D
produces another monadic functor
(r\mathbin{;}r^{\prime})\colon C\to E
. It is neither necessary nor sufficient that
r
be monadic:
(r\mathbin{;}r^{\prime})
may admit a left adjoint even when
r
does not; and
(r\mathbin{;}r^{\prime})
may not create the appropriate colimits even when
r
does. To understand the relationship between
r
,
r^{\prime}
, and
(r\mathbin{;}r^{\prime})
, it is enlightening to consider the generalisation to the relative setting. If
r^{\prime}
is
j
-monadic for some functor
j\colon A\to E
, we may ask when
(r\mathbin{;}r^{\prime})
is also
j
-monadic. However, it makes no sense to ask whether
r
, too, is
j
-monadic, because
r
and
j
have different codomains. Instead, it is most natural to ask whether
r
is monadic relative to
\ell^{\prime}\colon A\to D
, the left
j
-relative adjoint of
r^{\prime}
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

In fact, as we prove in
Section

6
, this is necessary and sufficient to ensure the
j
-monadicity of the composite
(r\mathbin{;}r^{\prime})
. This observation may be viewed as a pasting law for relatively monadic adjunctions: supposing that the triangle on the right is relatively monadic, the triangle on the left is relatively monadic if and only if the outer triangle is relatively monadic. This characterisation has a couple of advantages over the characterisation in terms of colimit creation: for one, it does not require that the roots
j
or
\ell^{\prime}
be dense, and the existence of a category of algebras can be derived rather than assumed
2
2

2

Recall that the existence of a
{\mathbb{V}}
-category of algebras for a
{\mathbb{V}}
-enriched (relative) monad requires the existence of certain limits in
{\mathbb{V}}
(cf.
[
AM24
, Corollary 8.20]
), and so is a nontrivial assumption for general
{\mathbb{V}}
.
. Furthermore, this characterisation appears to be new even for
j=1
, though we note that a similar observation appears in the work of
[
Wal70
, Theorem 1.5.5]
, of which our result may be seen as a refinement.

1.3.
Outline of the paper

In
Section

2
, we briefly recall the formal categorical concepts from
[
AM24
]
that will be fundamental to our study of relative monadicity. In
Section

3
, we introduce the notions of creation of limits and of colimits in a virtual equipment, and show that the forgetful tight-cell
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E
from the algebra object for a
j
-relative monad creates limits and
j
-absolute colimits (
Propositions

3.4
,
3.6
and
3.12
). In
Section

4
, we prove a formal relative monadicity theorem (
Theorems
4.7
and
′
‣
4.2
) and, as a consequence, show that the category of algebras for a relative monad
T
is the category of algebras for a monad if and only if the forgetful tight-cell
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E
admits a left adjoint (
Proposition

4.12
). In
Section

5
, we specialise the relative monadicity theorem to
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
and
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
for a well-behaved monoidal category
{\mathbb{V}}
, obtaining enriched relative monadicity and relative comonadicity theorems (
Theorems
5.2
and
co
). To demonstrate the application of the relative monadicity theorem, we use it to prove that (1) the category of algebras for a finitary algebraic theory is (relatively) monadic over
{\mathbf{Set}}
(
Example

5.6
); (2) that the category of algebras for a colimit-preserving monad on a free cocompletion is relatively monadic over the cocompletion (
Example

5.9
); and (3) that the category of algebras for a quantitative equational theory in the sense of
[
MPP16
]
is (relatively) monadic over
\mathbf{Met}
(
Example

5.10
). More generally, we show that the category of algebras for a
j
-theory in the sense of
[
LP23
]
is
j
-monadic (
Example

5.11
). Finally, in
Section

6
, we consider the interaction between the pasting law for relative adjunctions (
[
AM24
, Proposition 5.30]
) and relative monadicity, and thereby deduce necessary and sufficient conditions for the composite of a functor with a relatively monadic functor to itself be relatively monadic (
Theorem

6.5
).

Remark 1.1
.

In addition to
[
Die75
]
and
[
Lee77
]
,
[
Wal70
]
also established a series of relative monadicity theorems for unenriched relative monads with fully faithful roots
[
Wal70
, §2.3]
. However,
[
Wal70
]
imposes a number of additional assumptions on the functor
r\colon D\to E
that do not hold in general, and which are not appropriate for our purposes. We shall not pursue an explicit comparison to the theorems of
[
Wal70
]
in this paper.

Remark 1.2
.

After presenting an early version of this work to the Masaryk University Algebra Seminar, the authors were informed that John Bourke, Marcelo Fiore, and Richard Garner have, in unpublished joint work, independently established an enriched relative monadicity theorem.

2.
Formal categorical prerequisites

We shall work throughout the paper in the context of a virtual equipment
\mathbb{X}
, adopting the terminology and notation of
[
AM24
]
.
In this section, we shall briefly recall the fundamental concepts of formal category theory in a virtual equipment.
A more detailed introduction may be found in §2 – §3 of
[
AM24
]
.
The reader interested primarily in the applications of the relative monadicity theorem is encouraged to skip to
Section

5
, where we shall instantiate the formal theory in the context of the virtual equipment
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
of categories enriched in a monoidal category
{\mathbb{V}}
, and which may be read without familiarity with formal category theory.

A virtual equipment is, in particular, a virtual double category, which is a two-dimensional structure having
objects
;
tight-cells
(
\to
);
loose-cells
(
{\mathrel{\to}}
); and
2-cells
(
\Rightarrow
) of the following form (cf.
[
AM24
, Definition 2.1]
).

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B_{0}}}

For instance, the virtual double category
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
has as objects the (possibly large)
{\mathbb{V}}
-categories; as tight-cells the
{\mathbb{V}}
-functors; as loose-cells the
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors; and as 2-cells the
{\mathbb{V}}
-natural transformations, which are families of morphisms

\phi_{x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}}\colon p_{1}(x_{0},x_{1})\otimes\cdots\otimes p_{n}(x_{n-1},x_{n})\to q(|f_{0}|x_{0},|f_{n}|x_{n})

in
{\mathbb{V}}
for each
x_{0}\in|A_{0}|,\dots,x_{n}\in|A_{n}|
, satisfying several naturality laws
[
AM24
, Definition 8.1]
. For tight-cells
f\colon A\to B
and
g\colon B\to C
, we denote by
(f\mathbin{;}g)\colon A\to C
or
gf\colon A\to C
their composite. For loose-cells
p\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Y
and
q\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}Z
, we denote by
q\odot p\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Z
and
q\mathbin{{\odot}_{L}}p\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Z
their composite and left-composite (
[
AM24
, Definition 2.5]
) respectively, when they exist.

A virtual equipment (or simply
equipment
) is a virtual double category for which every object
A
admits a loose-identity
A(1,1)\colon A{\mathrel{\to}}A
(
[
AM24
, Definition 2.4]
); and for which, for every loose-cell
p\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Y
and tight-cells
g\colon W\to X
and
f\colon Z\to Y
, there is a restriction loose-cell
p(f,g)\colon W{\mathrel{\to}}Z
(
[
AM24
, Definition 2.7]
). We denote the restriction
A(1,1)(f,g)
along a loose-identity
A(1,1)
by
A(f,g)
: in
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
, this restriction is given by the hom-objects of
A
. Virtual equipments admit a string diagram calculus that we shall employ in some proofs, but are not required to understand the definitions or theorem statements.

One notable difference between the formal categorical setting and typical approaches to enriched category theory (cf.
[
Dub70
,
Kel82
]
) is that our limits and colimits are weighted by
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributors rather than
{\mathbb{V}}
-presheaves and
{\mathbb{V}}
-copresheaves: for a
{\mathbb{V}}
-distributor
p\colon X{\mathrel{\to}}Y
and
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor
f\colon Y\to Z
, the
p
-weighted colimit of
f
, when it exists, is a
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor

2.1.
Relative adjunctions, relative monads, and algebra objects

We recall the concepts introduced in
[
AM24
]
that are most relevant to our study of relative monadicity. The central concept is that of a relative monad, which is a generalisation of a monad that permits the carrier to be an arbitrary tight-cell, rather than an endo-tight-cell. Accordingly, a relative monad is parameterised by a tight-cell
j\colon A\to E
that plays the same role that the identity tight-cell plays for a non-relative monad.

Definition 2.1

(
[
AM24
, Definition 4.1]
)
.

A
relative monad
comprises

(2.1.(1))

a tight-cell
j\colon A\to E
, the
root
;

(2.1.(2))

a tight-cell
t\colon A\to E
, the
carrier
;

(2.1.(3))

a 2-cell
{\dagger}\colon E(j,t)\Rightarrow E(t,t)
, the
extension operator
;

(2.1.(4))

a 2-cell
\eta\colon j\Rightarrow t
, the
unit
,

satisfying associativity and left- and right-unit laws.
A
j
-relative monad
(or simply
j
-monad
) is a relative monad with root
j
.

Just as monads are typically induced by adjunctions, relative monads are typically induced by relative adjunctions. A relative adjunction is a generalisation of an adjunction that permits the left adjoint to have domain distinct from the codomain of the right adjoint.

Definition 2.2

(
[
AM24
, Definition 5.1]
)
.

A
relative adjunction
comprises

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

(2.2.(1))

a tight-cell
j\colon A\to E
, the
root
;

(2.2.(2))

a tight-cell
\ell\colon A\to C
, the
left (relative) adjoint
;

(2.2.(3))

a tight-cell
r\colon C\to E
, the
right (relative) adjoint
;

(2.2.(4))

an isomorphism
\sharp\colon C(\ell,1)\cong E(j,r)\penalty\mskip 6.0mu plus 1.0mu\mathpunct{}\nonscript\mkern-3.0mu{:}\mskip 2.0mu\flat
, the
(left- and right-) transposition operators
.

We denote by
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r
such data, and call
C
the
apex
. A
j
-relative adjunction
(or simply
j
-adjunction
) is a relative adjunction with root
j
.

Every
j
-adjunction
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r
induces a
j
-monad with carrier
(\ell\mathbin{;}r)\colon A\to E

[
AM24
, Theorem 5.24]
. A
j
-adjunction that induces a
j
-monad
T
is called a
resolution
of
T

[
AM24
, Definition 5.25]
.

Relative monads admit notions of algebra and algebra morphism analogous to those for non-relative monads. However, it is important to observe that, in the context of a virtual equipment, the appropriate notion of morphism of algebras is graded by a chain of loose-cells. This permits the consideration of morphisms between algebras with different domains, in contrast to morphisms of algebras in a 2-category
[
Str72
]
.

Definition 2.3

(
[
AM24
, Definitions 6.1 & 6.29]
)
.

Let
T
be a relative monad. An
algebra for
T
(or simply
T
-algebra
) comprises

(2.3.(1))

an object
D
, the
domain
;

(2.3.(2))

a tight-cell
e\colon D\to E
, the
carrier
;

(2.3.(3))

a 2-cell
{\rtimes}\colon E(j,e)\Rightarrow E(t,e)
, the
extension operator
,

satisfying compatibility laws with the extension operator
{\dagger}
and unit
\eta
for
T
.

Let
(e\colon D\to E,{\rtimes})
and
(e^{\prime}\colon D^{\prime}\to E,{\rtimes}^{\prime})
be
T
-algebras. A
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})
-graded
T
-algebra morphism
from
(e,{\rtimes})
to
(e^{\prime},{\rtimes}^{\prime})
is a 2-cell

\epsilon\colon E(1,e),p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\Rightarrow E(1,e^{\prime})

satisfying a compatibility law with the two extension operators
{\rtimes}
and
{\rtimes}^{\prime}
.

Remark 2.4

(
[
AM24
, Remark 6.30]
)
.

A
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})
-graded
T
-algebra morphism from
(e,{\rtimes})
to
(e^{\prime},{\rtimes}^{\prime})
is equivalently a 2-cell

\epsilon\colon p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\Rightarrow E(e,e^{\prime})

satisfying a compatibility law with the two extension operators
{\rtimes}
and
{\rtimes}^{\prime}
. We shall use the term
algebra morphism
to refer to both forms of 2-cell interchangeably.

An algebra object for a relative monad
T
is a universal
T
-algebra. In
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
, this corresponds to the
{\mathbb{V}}
-category of
T
-algebras
[
AM24
, §8.3]
. Algebra objects are the central object of interest for the relative monadicity theorem.

Definition 2.5

(
[
AM24
, Definition 6.33]
)
.

Let
T
be a relative monad. A
T
-algebra
(u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E,{\rtimes}_{T})
is an

algebra object
for
T
when

(2.5.(1))

for every
T

(e\colon D\to E,{\rtimes})

{\langle\rangle}_{(e,{\rtimes})}\colon D\to\mathbf{Alg}(T)

{\langle\rangle}_{(e,{\rtimes})}\mathbin{;}u_{T}=e

{\rtimes}_{T}(1,{\langle\rangle}_{(e,{\rtimes})})={\rtimes}

(2.5.(2))

for every graded
T
-algebra morphism
\epsilon\colon E(1,e),p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\Rightarrow E(1,e^{\prime})

{\langle\rangle}_{\epsilon}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)(1,{\langle\rangle}_{(e,{\rtimes})}),p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\Rightarrow\mathbf{Alg}(T)(1,{\langle\rangle}_{(e^{\prime},{\rtimes}^{\prime})})
such that:

3.
Creation of limits, colimits, and isomorphisms

We begin with some elementary observations on the creation of limits and certain colimits by forgetful functors from categories of algebras for relative monads.

3.1.
Strict creation

We first introduce the notion of strict creation of weighted limits and colimits, which will be important in the strict relative monadicity theorem (
Section

4.1
). We then introduce creation of isomorphisms, and non-strict creation of limits and colimits in
Section

3.2
, which will be important in the non-strict relative monadicity theorem (
Section

4.2
). For the notions of weighted limit and weighted colimit in an equipment, see
[
AM24
, §3.2]
.

Remark 3.1
.

Since there is substantial inconsistency in the literature regarding which of strict or non-strict creation (and consequently monadicity) should be taken as fundamental, we shall be explicit about strictness throughout; the unqualified terms are used only informally.

Definition 3.3

(
[
AM24
, Definition 3.21]
)
.

Let
p\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a loose-cell and let
j\colon A\to E
and
f\colon Z\to E

.

that specialise appropriately to enriched categories of algebras. In fact,

and

{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
.

3.2.
Non-strict creation

Next, we consider the non-strict creation of limits and colimits, which will be important in the non-strict relative monadicity theorem (
Section

4.2
). It will be useful to observe that non-strict creation of (co)limits is implied by strict creation of (co)limits together with the creation (or, equivalently, the reflection) of isomorphisms.

Definition 3.9
.

A tight-cell
g\colon W\to X
is
conservative
if, for each parallel pair of tight-cells
f_{1},f_{2}\colon Z\rightrightarrows W
and each 2-cell
\phi\colon f_{1}\Rightarrow f_{2}
, invertibility of
(\phi\mathbin{;}g)
implies invertibility of
\phi
.

Lemma 3.10
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a tight-cell and let
T
be
j
-monad admitting an algebra object
(u_{T},{\rtimes}_{T})
.
The tight-cell
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E
is conservative.

Proof.

Let
f_{1},f_{2}\colon Z\rightrightarrows\mathbf{Alg}(T)
be a parallel pair of tight-cells and let
\phi\colon f_{1}\Rightarrow f_{2}
be a 2-cell. Suppose that
(\phi\mathbin{;}u_{T})
admits an inverse. Since
(\phi\mathbin{;}u_{T})
is an algebra morphism, so is its inverse, so that the inverse factors uniquely through
u_{T}
by the universal property of
\mathbf{Alg}(T)
.
∎

We shall mark with a prime (
′
) the non-strict variants of definitions and results corresponding to strict variants.

Definition
3.2
′
.

Let
p\colon Y{\mathrel{\to}}Z
be a loose-cell, and let
f\colon Z\to W
and
g\colon W\to X

p
-cocone corresponding to
\phi
is colimiting if and only if the
p
-cocone corresponding to
(\phi\mathbin{;}g)
is colimiting. The limit case follows analogously.
∎

The non-strict analogues of
Propositions

3.4
and
3.6
follow.

Proposition 3.12
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a tight-cell and let
T
be
j
-monad admitting an algebra object
(u_{T},{\rtimes}_{T})
.
The tight-cell
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E
non-strictly creates limits and
j
-absolute colimits.

Proof.

Follows directly from
Propositions

3.4
,
3.6
,
3.10
and
3.11
.
∎

Remark 3.13
.

From
Proposition

3.12
, we recover
[
Par71
, Theorem 7.2]
for non-relative monads in
{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
.

4.
Relative monadicity

In this section, we establish a relative monadicity theorem (
Theorem

4.7
(
′
)) for relative monads with dense roots. We start by reviewing our approach to strictness.

The universal property of an algebra object (
Definition

2.5
) identifies it up to isomorphism. Consequently, every object isomorphic to an algebra object is itself an algebra object for the same relative monad. This aligns with the general philosophy of
[
AM24
]
, where we are concerned with
categories
of relative monads, in which the appropriate notion of indistinguishability is isomorphism (rather than with 2-categories or virtual double categories of relative monads, in which the appropriate notion of indistinguishability would be equivalence). Our primary interest in relative monadicity thus concerns
strict
relative monadicity, characterising when a tight-cell
r\colon D\to E
is isomorphic in
\underline{\mathbb{X}}/E
to the forgetful tight-cell for a
j
-monad.

We therefore proceed to first establish a strict relative monadicity theorem, as it requires more care than the non-strict variant. Since a non-strict relative monadicity theorem is also of interest, we provide one in
Section

4.2
. However, as the proof strategy is identical to the strict case, up to appropriate replacement of identities with isomorphisms, our treatment of the non-strict case is succinct.

We shall now outline our proof strategy, and discuss the subtleties that arise in the formal setting. Fix a tight-cell
j\colon A\to E
. Given a tight-cell
r\colon D\to E
, we should like to characterise when it exhibits the forgetful tight-cell for an algebra object for a
j
-monad. Assuming that algebra objects exist, we may reformulate this condition, using the universal property, into the following.

Definition 4.1
.

A tight-cell
r\colon D\to E
is
strictly
j
-relatively monadic
(alternatively
strictly monadic relative to
j
, or simply
strictly
j
-monadic
) if it admits a left
j
-adjoint, the induced
j
-monad
T
admits an algebra object, and the comparison tight-cell
{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}\colon D\to\mathbf{Alg}(T)
is an isomorphism.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{Alg}(T)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u_{T}}

Explicitly, this means that, to exhibit
r
as the forgetful tight-cell for an algebra object, we must construct a tight-cell
\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to D
that is inverse to the comparison tight-cell
{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}
. To do so, we shall observe that
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E
can be exhibited as a certain weighted colimit (
Proposition

4.3
). Supposing that
r
creates this colimit, the lifting then provides the desired inverse. Furthermore, the weighted colimit in question will be shown to be
j
-absolute, and so creation of
j
-absolute colimits provides both a necessary and sufficient condition for
j
-monadicity, by
Proposition

3.4
.

Note, however, that when the
j
-monad induced by
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r
does not admit an algebra object, such an approach is not possible, as there is no comparison tight-cell that we may ask to be invertible.
The relative monadicity theorem we prove in this section is therefore a
detection
result, rather than a
construction
result: it characterises when a tight-cell is relatively monadic
assuming that an algebra object exists
. This is not a trivial assumption even for enriched (non-relative) monadicity. However, it is also not a particularly restrictive assumption, as algebra objects typically exist in settings of interest (for instance, when the enriching category
{\mathbb{V}}
is closed and admits enough limits
[
AM24
, Corollary 8.20]
).

4.1.
Strict relative monadicity

The first step towards a relative monadicity theorem is to identify the appropriate colimits for creation. To do so, we observe in the following proposition that, for dense
j
, a right-morphism of relative adjunctions
(\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r)\to(\ell^{\prime}\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r^{\prime})
, exhibits
r^{\prime}
as a left extension of
r
(cf.
[
AM24
, Proposition 5.10]
).
In particular, this is true of morphisms of resolutions, in which the 2-cell
\rho
below is the identity (
[
AM24
, Definition 5.23]
).

Remark 4.2
.

Recall that, in general, a right-morphism
(c,\rho)\colon(\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r)\to(\ell^{\prime}\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r^{\prime})
comprises a tight-cell
c\colon C\to C^{\prime}
commuting with the left relative adjoints, and a 2-cell
\rho\colon r\Rightarrow(c\mathbin{;}r^{\prime})
compatible with the transposition operators
[
AM24
, Definition 5.18]
. However, when
j
is dense, the 2-cell
\rho
is uniquely determined by the transposition operators
[
AM24
, Lemma 5.21]
. This is the case in the following proposition.

Proposition 4.3
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a dense tight-cell and let
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r
be a
j
-adjunction. Consider tight-cells
c\colon C\to C^{\prime}
and
r^{\prime}\colon C^{\prime}\to E
, and a 2-cell
\rho\colon r\Rightarrow(c\mathbin{;}r^{\prime})
. Define
\ell^{\prime}\mathrel{:=}(\ell\mathbin{;}c)
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho}

The following are equivalent.

(4.3.(1))

\ell^{\prime}\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r^{\prime}
, and
(c,\rho)\colon(\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r)\to(\ell^{\prime}\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r^{\prime})
is a right-morphism of
j
-adjunctions.

(4.3.(2))

\rho
exhibits
r^{\prime}
as the
j
-absolute left extension
c\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}r
.

Proof.

Observe that, since
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r
, the loose-composite
E(j,r)\odot C^{\prime}(c,1)
is isomorphic to
C^{\prime}(\ell^{\prime},1)
:

C^{\prime}(\ell^{\prime},1)=C^{\prime}(c\ell,1)\cong C(\ell,1)\odot C^{\prime}(c,1)\cong E(j,r)\odot C^{\prime}(c,1)

(1)
\implies
(2). Since
\ell^{\prime}\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r^{\prime}
, we have

E(j,r^{\prime})\cong C^{\prime}(\ell^{\prime},1)\cong E(j,r)\odot C^{\prime}(c,1)

from which the result follows by
[
AM24
, Lemma 3.23]
using that
j
is dense.

(2)
\implies
(1). We have

C^{\prime}(\ell^{\prime},1)\cong E(j,r)\odot C^{\prime}(c,1)\cong E(j,c\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}r)

using
j
-absoluteness and
[
AM24
, Lemma 3.23]
, so that
\ell^{\prime}\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r^{\prime}
. That
(c,\rho)
forms a right-morphism follows from the definition of
\ell^{\prime}\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r^{\prime}
.
∎

Since the left extensions of
Proposition

4.3
are
j
-absolute, they are created by the forgetful tight-cell
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E
of any algebra object for a
j
-monad. We shall show shortly that creation of such colimits is sufficient to imply
j
-monadicity. The observation above motivates the following definition.

Definition 4.4
.

Let
r\colon D\to E
be tight-cell. An
r
-extension
is a left extension
c\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}r
, for some tight-cell
c
with domain
D
.

The core technical lemma in the proof of the relative monadicity theorem is the following.

Lemma 4.5
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a dense tight-cell, and let
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r
be a resolution of a
j
-monad
T
. If
r
strictly creates
j
-absolute
r
-extensions, then every morphism of resolutions with domain
(\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r)
admits a retraction
c\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1_{C}
.

Proof.

Let
c\colon(\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r)\to(\ell^{\prime}\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r^{\prime})
be a morphism of resolutions of
T
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{\prime}}

By
Proposition

4.3
, using density of
j
, we have
r^{\prime}\cong c\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}r
.
This left extension is a
j
-absolute
r
-extension, so is strictly created by
r
.
Hence there is a unique pair of a tight-cell
d\colon C^{\prime}\to C
and 2-cell

\eta\colon 1_{C}\Rightarrow c\mathbin{;}d
such that
d\mathbin{;}r=r^{\prime}
and

\eta\mathbin{;}r=1_{r}
. Furthermore,
\eta
exhibits
d
as the left extension
c\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1_{C}
.
We shall prove that
c\mathbin{;}d=1_{C}
: this implies that
d
is a morphism of resolutions, and hence is a retraction of
c
in the category of resolutions of
T
, because
\ell\mathbin{;}c=\ell^{\prime}
.

The identity 2-cell
1_{r}
exhibits
r
as the
j
-absolute
r
-extension
1_{C}\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}r
trivially.
This left extension is strictly created by
r
, so there is a unique pair
(x,\chi)
of a tight-cell
x\colon C\to C
and 2-cell
\chi\colon 1_{C}\Rightarrow x
such that
x\mathbin{;}r=r
and
\chi\mathbin{;}r=1_{r}
.
Clearly
(1_{C},1_{1_{C}})
is such a pair, but, by the above, and the fact that
c\mathbin{;}r^{\prime}=r
, so is
((c\mathbin{;}d),\eta)
.
Hence
c\mathbin{;}d=1_{C}
as required.
∎

In passing, we note that, when algebra objects exist, a relative adjunction is a terminal resolution if and only if its right relative adjoint exhibits an algebra object
[
AM24
, Corollary 6.41]
. However, if algebra objects are not known to exist, terminality is a weaker condition than exhibiting an algebra object. The following corollary of
Lemma

4.5
is useful when terminality is sufficient. One could use this fact to give a proof of the relative monadicity theorem; however, we shall give a different proof that generalises more easily to the non-strict setting.

Corollary 4.6
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a dense tight-cell, let
T
be a
j
-monad admitting a terminal resolution
f\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}u
, and let
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r
be a resolution of
T
. If
r
strictly creates
j
-absolute
r
-extensions, then
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r
is a terminal resolution of
T
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces M}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}}

Proof.

Since
(f\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}u)
is terminal, there is a unique morphism
(\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r)\to(f\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}u)
. By
Lemma

4.5
, this morphism is a split monomorphism, because
r
strictly creates
j
-absolute
r
-extensions. However, every split monomorphism into a terminal object is an isomorphism, so
(\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r)\cong(f\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}u)
.
∎

The relative monadicity theorem follows essentially directly from
Propositions

3.4
and
4.5
.

Theorem 4.7

(Relative monadicity)
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a dense tight-cell. A tight-cell
r\colon D\to E
is strictly
j
-monadic if and only if
r
admits a left
j
-adjoint, the induced
j
-monad admits an algebra object, and
r
strictly creates
j
-absolute
r
-extensions.

Proof.

If
r
is strictly
j
-monadic, then it admits a left
j
-adjoint for which the induced
j
-monad has an algebra object, by definition. Furthermore,
r
is the composite of an isomorphism with
u_{T}
, hence strictly creates
j
-absolute
r
-extensions by
Proposition

3.4
. For the converse, observe that
r
and
u_{T}
both strictly create
j
-absolute
r
-extensions, so that
{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}
and
{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1_{D}
exhibit
D
and
\mathbf{Alg}(T)
as retracts of one another by
Lemma

4.5
, and hence
{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}
is invertible.
∎

We may additionally relax the class of colimits that
r
need create in order to be
j
-monadic, so that the class is independent of
r
.

Corollary 4.8
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a dense tight-cell. A tight-cell
r\colon D\to E
is strictly
j
-monadic if and only if
r
admits a left
j
-adjoint, the induced
j
-monad admits an algebra object, and
r
strictly creates
j
-absolute colimits.

Proof.

Follows directly from
Theorem

4.7
, since
u_{T}
strictly creates all
j
-absolute colimits by
Proposition

3.4
.
∎

In practice,
Corollary

4.8
is often more convenient: for instance, in
Section

5
, we shall give a simple characterisation of the
j
-absolute colimits in
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
for a well-behaved monoidal category
{\mathbb{V}}
. However, in
Proposition

4.12
we shall give an example of a situation in which the sharper result of
Theorem

4.7
is useful.

Remark 4.9
.

The assumption that
j
be dense in the statement of
Theorem

4.7
is necessary. For instance, denoting by
0
the empty category, every functor
r\colon D\to E
(for arbitrary categories
D
and
E
) is right adjoint to the unique functor
[]_{D}\colon 0\to D
relative to the unique functor
[]_{E}\colon 0\to E
, which is dense only when
E
is indiscrete.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces[]_{D}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces[]_{E}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

The trivial
[]_{E}
-monad is the unique
[]_{E}
-monad. Consequently,
r\colon D\to E
is
[]_{E}
-monadic if and only if it is an isomorphism
[
AM24
, Proposition 6.42]
. However, every colimit in
E
is
[]_{E}
-absolute (by
Lemma

5.1
below), and so any non-invertible functor
r\colon D\to E
that strictly creates colimits is a counterexample to the statement of
Theorem

4.7
. We leave as an open question whether there are sufficient conditions for relative monadicity in the absence of density.

Remark 4.10
.

For each tight-cell
j\colon A\to E
, the category of
j
-monads is equipped with a fully faithful partial functor
u_{{({-})}}\colon\mathbf{RMnd}(j){}^{\mathrm{op}}\hookrightarrow\underline{\mathbb{X}}/E
to the category of slices over
E
, sending each relative monad
T
that admits an algebra object to the forgetful tight-cell
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E
from its algebra object
[
AM24
, Corollary 6.40]
. Abstractly, the relative monadicity theorem may be seen as a characterisation of the essential image of this partial functor, consequently exhibiting an equivalence between the full subcategory of
\mathbf{RMnd}(j){}^{\mathrm{op}}
spanned by
j
-monads admitting algebra objects, and the full subcategory of
\underline{\mathbb{X}}/E
spanned by
j
-monadic tight-cells.

Remark 4.11
.

Algebra objects for monads in a 2-category (which are weaker than algebra objects for monads in an equipment
[
AM24
, 61]
) can be characterised representably in terms of algebra objects for monads in the 2-category
\mathbf{Cat}

[
Str72
, Theorem 8]
. Consequently, monadicity for monads in a 2-category
\mathcal{K}
may be characterised representably in terms of monadicity in
\mathbf{Cat}

[
Str72
, Corollary 8.1]
.
[
Woo85
, Proposition 22]
makes use of this characterisation to give a formal monadicity theorem, which is, in essence, an objectwise version of
[
Bec66
]
’s monadicity theorem
[
Bec66
]
.
[
Woo85
]
’s monadicity theorem is thus of an entirely different nature to
Theorem

4.7
, which is a characterisation internal to the equipment
\mathbb{X}
.
A consequence is that
Theorem

4.7
, in contrast to
[
Woo85
]
’s monadicity theorem, directly specialises to the monadicity theorem for enriched monads.

A particularly useful consequence of the relative monadicity theorem is the following proposition, which relates algebra objects for relative monads that have different roots. Observe that the proof follows easily from
Theorem

4.7
, whereas a proof based on
Corollary

4.8
is less straightforward.

Proposition 4.12
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
and
j^{\prime}\colon E\to I
be tight-cells, and let
T
be a
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-monad admitting an algebra object. Suppose that
j^{\prime}
is dense. Then
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E^{\prime}
is strictly
j^{\prime}
-monadic if and only if it admits a left
j^{\prime}
-adjoint and the induced
j^{\prime}
-monad admits an algebra object.

Proof.

The only if direction is trivial. For the other direction, observe that every
j^{\prime}
-absolute
r
-extension is a
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-absolute
r
-extension, since every right-morphism of
j^{\prime}
-adjunctions induces a right-morphism of
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-adjunctions by precomposing
j

[
AM24
, Proposition 5.29]
. Therefore, since
u_{T}
strictly creates
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-absolute
r
-extensions, it strictly creates, in particular,
j^{\prime}
-absolute
r
-extensions, from which the result follows by
Theorem

4.7
.
∎

In particular, if every monad admits an algebra object, we obtain that the algebra object for a relative monad
T
is the algebra object for a monad whenever the forgetful tight-cell
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to E
admits a left adjoint.

4.2.
Non-strict relative monadicity

We now briefly discuss the case of non-strict relative monadicity. While strict relative monadicity is often the appropriate notion, there are situations in which it is convenient to consider a property that is invariant under equivalence. This motivates the following definition.

Definition
4.1
′
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a tight-cell. A tight-cell
r\colon D\to E
is
non-strictly
j
-relatively monadic
(alternatively
non-strictly monadic relative to
j
, or simply
non-strictly
j
-monadic
) if it admits a left
j
-adjoint, the induced
j
-monad
T
admits an algebra object, and the comparison tight-cell
{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}\colon D\to\mathbf{Alg}(T)
is an equivalence.

Informally, a characterisation of non-strict relative monadicity is obtained by relaxing
Theorem

4.7
through the replacement of the equality of tight-cells by isomorphism, and thereby asking for non-strict creation of colimits rather than strict creation. With respect to the proof strategy, there is one notable difference to the strict case. While, just as in the strict setting, the comparison tight-cell
{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}\colon D\to\mathbf{Alg}(T)
is a morphism of resolutions, the tight-cell
\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to D
constructed via the non-strict creation of colimits only commutes with the left and right adjoints up to isomorphism. However, once this subtlety is taken into account, the proof then proceeds in essentially the same way as the strict case.

Below, our proof follows the structure of the strict case. Each statement is numbered according to its non-strict pair and marked with a prime (
′
) to denote non-strictness.

Lemma
4.5
′
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a dense tight-cell, and let
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r
be a resolution of a
j
-monad
T
. If
r
non-strictly creates
j
-absolute
r
-extensions, then every tight-cell
c\colon C\to C^{\prime}
rendering pseudo-commutative the diagram on the left below admits a pseudo-retraction
c\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1_{C}
rendering pseudo-commutative the diagram on the right below.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces c\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1_{C}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}

Proof (sketch).

We have a
j
-adjunction
(\ell\mathbin{;}c)\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r^{\prime}
using
\ell^{\prime}\cong(\ell\mathbin{;}c)
.
Since
j
is dense, there is a unique right-morphism
(c,\rho)\colon(\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r)\to((\ell\mathbin{;}c)\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r^{\prime})
of
j
-adjunctions (cf.
Remark

4.2
).
Therefore, by
Proposition

4.3
,
\rho
exhibits
r^{\prime}
as the
j
-absolute
r
-extension
c\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}r
.
The proof of
Lemma

4.5
then carries through with respect to non-strict creation of colimits after replacing the equalities of tight-cells with isomorphisms.
∎

Theorem
4.7
′
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a dense tight-cell. A tight-cell
r\colon D\to E
is non-strictly
j
-monadic if and only if
r
admits a left
j
-adjoint, the induced
j
-monad admits an algebra object, and
r
non-strictly creates
j
-absolute
r
-extensions.

Proof.

If
r
is non-strictly
j
-monadic, then it admits a left
j
-adjoint for which the induced
j
-monad has an algebra object, by definition. Furthermore,
r
is the composite of an equivalence with
u_{T}
, hence non-strictly creates
j
-absolute
r
-extensions by
Proposition

3.12
. For the converse, observe that
r
and
u_{T}
both non-strictly create
j
-absolute
r
-extensions, so that
{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}
and
{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}\mathbin{{\rhd}\mathclap{\mspace{-17.5mu}\cdot}}1_{D}
exhibit
D
and
\mathbf{Alg}(T)
as pseudo-retracts of one another by
′
‣
Section

4.2
, and hence that
{\langle\rangle}_{\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r}
is an equivalence.
∎

Corollary
4.8
′
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
be a dense tight-cell. A tight-cell
r\colon D\to E
is non-strictly
j
-monadic if and only if
r
admits a left
j
-adjoint, the induced
j
-monad admits an algebra object, and
r
non-strictly creates
j
-absolute colimits.

Proof.

Follows directly from
′
‣
Section

4.2
together with
Proposition

3.12
.
∎

Equivalently, in the statements of
′
‣
Sections

4.2
and
′
‣
4.2
, rather than ask that
r
non-strictly create the requisite colimits, we could ask for
r
to be conservative and preserve the requisite colimits (using
Lemma

3.11
and that conservative tight-cells are closed under equivalences and composition), which is often more convenient in practice.

Proposition
4.12
′
.

Let
j\colon A\to E
and
j^{\prime}\colon E\to I
be tight-cells and suppose that
j^{\prime}
is dense. A non-strictly
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-monadic tight-cell
r\colon D\to E^{\prime}
is non-strictly
j^{\prime}
-monadic if and only if it admits a left
j^{\prime}
-adjoint and the induced
j^{\prime}
-monad admits an algebra object.

Proof.

The proof of
Proposition

4.12
carries through with respect to non-strict creation of colimits.
∎

5.
Enriched relative monadicity

Instantiating
Theorem

4.7
(
′
) and its corollaries in the equipment
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
of categories enriched in a monoidal category
{\mathbb{V}}
(
[
AM24
, Definition 8.1]
), we immediately obtain a relative monadicity theorem for enriched relative monads. Under some additional assumptions on
{\mathbb{V}}
, we may make some simplifications.
We first make note of the following characterisation of
j
-absolute colimits, which is a special case of
[
AM24
, Lemma 8.10]
.
Below, when they exist, we write
\mathcal{P}A
for the
{\mathbb{V}}
-category of presheaves on a
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
A
, and write
n_{j}\colon E\to\mathcal{P}A
for the nerve of a
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor
j\colon A\to E
, which is defined by
n_{j}e\mathrel{:=}E(j{-},e)
. Dually, we write
\mathcal{Q}Z
for the
{\mathbb{V}}
-category of copresheaves on a
{\mathbb{V}}
-category
Z
, and write
m_{i}\colon U\to\mathcal{Q}Z
for the co-nerve of a
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor
i\colon Z\to U
, which is defined by
m_{i}u\mathrel{:=}U(u,i{-})
.

Lemma 5.1
.

Let
{\mathbb{V}}
be a complete left- and right-closed monoidal category and let
j\colon A\to E
be a
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor with small domain.
Given a
{\mathbb{V}}

and

in
E
is
j
-absolute exactly when it is preserved by the nerve
n_{j}\colon E\to\mathcal{P}A
.

Proof.

Since
A
is small,
\mathcal{P}A
exists by
[
GP99
, §3]
, and the result follows by
[
AM24
, Lemma 8.10]
.
∎

We spell out
Corollary

4.8
(
′
) in the equipments
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
and
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}{}^{\mathrm{co}}
, where
{\mathbb{V}}
is a well-behaved monoidal category, using the characterisation of
j
-absolute colimits above.

Theorem 5.2

(Enriched relative monadicity)
.

Let
{\mathbb{V}}
be a complete left- and right-closed monoidal category and let
j\colon A\to E
be a dense
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor with small domain.
A
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor
r\colon D\to E
is (non)strictly
j
-monadic if and only if
r
admits a left
j
-adjoint and (non)strictly creates those colimits that are preserved by the nerve
n_{j}\colon E\to\mathcal{P}A
.

Proof.

Since
A
is small,
{\mathbb{V}}
-categories of algebras for
j
-monads exist by
[
AM24
, Corollary 8.20]
.
The result then follows directly from
Corollary

4.8
(
′
) together with
Lemma

5.1
.
∎

Theorem
5.2
co

(Enriched relative comonadicity)
.

Let
{\mathbb{V}}
be a complete left- and right-closed monoidal category and let
i\colon Z\to U
be a codense
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor with small domain.
A
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor
\ell\colon W\to U
is (non)strictly
i
-comonadic if and only if
\ell
admits a right
i
-coadjoint and (non)strictly creates those limits that are preserved by the co-nerve
m_{i}\colon U\to\mathcal{Q}Z
.

Proof.

Since
A
is small, copresheaf
{\mathbb{V}}
-categories exist, as do
{\mathbb{V}}
-categories of coalgebras for
i
-comonads by
[
AM24
, Theorem 8.23]
. The result then follows as for
Theorem

5.2
.
∎

Remark 5.3
.

When
A
is large, presheaf
{\mathbb{V}}
-categories can no longer be assumed to exist, and so
j
-absoluteness cannot be characterised in terms of the nerve without a change of enrichment base. In this case
Theorem

4.7
(
′
) and
Corollary

4.8
(
′
) may be used directly.

From
Theorem

5.2
, taking
j=1
, we recover the unenriched monadicity theorem of
[
Par69
]

[
Par69a
,
Par69
,
Par71
]
, which is a reformulation of the unenriched monadicity theorem of
[
Bec66
]
in terms of absolute colimits; as well as an analogous characterisation of enriched monadicity (cf.
[
Bun69
,
Dub70
]
). Taking
j
to be dense and fully faithful, we recover the unenriched relative monadicity theorems of
[
Die75
]

[
Die75
,
Die76
]
and
[
Lee77
, Corollary 2.8]
.

Remark 5.4
.

It does not appear to be possible to obtain a characterisation of relative monadicity in terms of contractible coequalisers without much stronger assumptions on the root
j
that seldom hold in examples of interest other than
j=1
; we do not pursue such a characterisation.

Remark 5.5
.

The formal relative monadicity theorem
Corollary

4.8
(
′
) applies to a relative monad
T
with a dense root as soon as
T
admits an algebra object. Therefore, establishing a relative monadicity theorem in a given virtual equipment
\mathbb{X}
reduces to establishing the existence of algebra objects in
\mathbb{X}
. In
[
AM24
]
, the existence of algebra objects was studied only for the virtual equipment
{\mathbb{V}}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
. However, as we shall show in future work, the proof given there carries through with minor modifications in the more general context of the virtual equipment
\textup{\sagittarius}{\mathbf{\mathbb{M}nd}}(\mathbb{X})
of loose-monads and modules in a virtual double category
\mathbb{X}
with restrictions (cf.
[
CS10
, Proposition 7.4]
). In this way, we shall obtain relative monadicity theorems for other notions of category, such as internal categories and generalised multicategories, as well as for more general notions of enriched category
[
Lei99
]
.

5.1.
Examples

We now demonstrate the usefulness of the relative monadicity theorem by presenting several prototypical situations in which the theorem may be applied.

In the first situation we present, one has a notion of theory and an accompanying notion of algebra. For instance, we may show that the category of algebras for a finitary algebraic theory is monadic relative to the inclusion of finite sets into small sets (cf.
[
Lin66
,
Lin69
,
Die75
,
Die76
]
).

Example 5.6

(Algebraic theories induce monads)
.

Denote by
{\mathbb{F}}
the free category with strict finite coproducts on a single object
1
. The inclusion
j\colon{\mathbb{F}}\simeq{\mathbf{FinSet}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}}
of finite ordinals into small sets exhibits a cocompletion under sifted colimits, and is hence dense and fully faithful.

Now consider a finitary algebraic theory
k\colon{\mathbb{F}}\to K
in the sense of
[
Law63
, Chapter 2]
, i.e. an identity-on-objects functor preserving finite coproducts. The category of algebras for
k
is, up to equivalence, the category
\mathbf{Cart}[K{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]
of finite-product-preserving functors from
K{}^{\mathrm{op}}
to
{\mathbf{Set}}
. The forgetful functor, which we denote by
u_{k}\colon\mathbf{Cart}[K{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]\to{\mathbf{Set}}
, is the composite of
\mathbf{Cart}[k{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]
with the equivalence
\mathbf{Cart}[{\mathbb{F}}{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]\simeq{\mathbf{Set}}
. Since
K
has finite coproducts,
u_{k}
is a continuous and sifted-cocontinuous functor between locally strongly finitely presentable categories
[
AR01
]
, and consequently admits a left adjoint
f_{k}\colon{\mathbf{Set}}\to\mathbf{Cart}[K{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]
. Denoting by
\sigma_{L}\colon K\hookrightarrow\mathbf{Cart}[K{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]
the Yoneda embedding, we therefore have the following diagram in
\mathbf{CAT}
, in which the rightmost square is a pseudopullback.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces K}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{Cart}[K{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[K{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbb{F}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{Set}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[{\mathbb{F}}{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u_{k}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{\sigma_{K}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{j}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces[k{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces k}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{k}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma_{K}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\it{ps.\;pb}}

Since
k
is identity-on-objects,
[k{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbf{Set}}]
is an amnestic isofibration and strictly creates colimits. By the former property, the pseudopullback is equivalent to the strict pullback
[
JS93
, Corollary 1]
.
The forgetful functor
u_{k}
therefore non-strictly creates those colimits that
n_{j}
preserves
[
Sch72
, Proposition 21.7.2(c)]
, which are precisely the
j
-absolute colimits by
Lemma

5.1
. By
[
AM24
, Proposition 5.29]
, we have
(j\mathbin{;}f_{k})\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}u_{k}
and so
u_{k}
is
j
-monadic by
Theorem

5.2
. Furthermore, by
′
‣
Section

4.2
, it is additionally non-strictly monadic. Every finitary algebraic theory therefore induces both a
j
-monad, and a sifted-cocontinuous monad on
{\mathbf{Set}}
– the former obtained by precomposing the latter by
j

[
AM24
, Proposition 5.36]
– whose categories of algebras are concretely equivalent.

More generally, the methods of
Example

5.6
may be used to show that, for an arity class
\kappa
in the sense of
[
Shu12
, Definition 2.2]
(for instance, any regular cardinal), the category of algebras for a
\kappa
-ary algebraic theory is monadic relative to
{\mathbf{Set}}_{\kappa}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}}
, the full subcategory inclusion of the
\kappa
-small sets. When
\kappa={\mathbb{N}}
, we recover finitary algebraic theories; and when
\kappa
is the cardinality of the universe, we recover infinitary algebraic theories. Another useful case is given by taking
\kappa=\{1\}
, as in the following example.

Example 5.7
.

A unary algebraic theory is an identity-on-objects functor with domain
1
, and is understood syntactically to be a theory presented solely by unary operations. Concretely, each unary algebraic theory is equivalent to a monoid
M
, viewed as a one-object category, and its category of algebras is the presheaf category
{\mathbf{Set}}^{M{}^{\mathrm{op}}}
of right-actions of
M
(sometimes called
right
M
-sets
). Consequently, a functor is
(1\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}})
-monadic precisely when its domain is equivalent to a presheaf category on a single object, and its action is given by evaluation at that unique object.

Alternatively, we may give a characterisation via the relative monadicity theorem. Observe that the nerve of
1\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}}
is isomorphic to the identity functor on
{\mathbf{Set}}
. Hence every colimit is
(1\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}})
-absolute. A functor
u\colon D\to{\mathbf{Set}}
is therefore
(1\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}})
-monadic if and only if it creates colimits and admits a left
(1\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}})
-adjoint. This latter condition holds exactly when
u
is corepresentable, i.e. when there exists an object
d\in|D|
such that
u\cong D(d,{-})
.

Examples

5.6
and
5.7
demonstrate the typical relationship between monadicity relative to different functors. Suppose that we have functors
j\colon A\to E
and
j^{\prime}\colon E\to I
. In general,
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-monadicity is neither stronger nor weaker than
j^{\prime}
-monadicity:
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-adjointness is a weaker property than
j^{\prime}
-adjointness, but creation of the requisite
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-absolute colimits is a stronger property than creation of the requisite
j^{\prime}
-absolute colimits. However, in many cases of interest, a
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-monadic functor will admit a left
j^{\prime}
-adjoint, in which case
Proposition

4.12
(
′
) will apply.

Example 5.8
.

Consider the inclusions
j\colon 1\hookrightarrow{\mathbb{F}}
and
j^{\prime}\colon{\mathbb{F}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}}
, so that
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-monadicity is the
(1\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}})
-monadicity of
Example

5.7
and
j^{\prime}
-monadicity is the
({\mathbb{F}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}})
-monadicity of
Example

5.6
. By the adjoint functor theorem, the forgetful functor from the category of algebras for any unary algebraic theory admits a left adjoint, and is thus monadic, and hence also
j^{\prime}
-monadic. Thus
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-monadicity implies
j^{\prime}
-monadicity. The converse is not true in general: although the forgetful functor from the category of algebras for a finitary algebraic theory admits a left adjoint, and thus also a
(j\mathbin{;}j^{\prime})
-adjoint, it will not create all colimits in general. For instance, the underlying set of a coproduct of monoids is not the coproduct of their underlying sets.

More generally, for arity classes
\kappa\subseteq\kappa^{\prime}
, the methods above may be used to show that the category of algebras for a
\kappa
-ary algebraic theory is always
({\mathbf{Set}}_{\kappa^{\prime}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}})
-monadic. Taking
\kappa^{\prime}
to be the cardinality of the universe, every
\kappa
-ary algebraic theory is seen to induce a monad on
{\mathbf{Set}}
of rank
\kappa
.

In the second situation we present, one has a class of weights
\Phi
, and a monad
T
on a free
\Phi
-cocompletion
\Phi(A)
, for which
T
preserves
\Phi
-weighted colimits. In this case, the category of algebras for
T
is monadic relative to the cocompletion
A\to\Phi(A)
.

Example 5.9
.

Let
\Phi
be a class of weights, let
A
be a small
{\mathbb{V}}
-category admitting a free cocompletion
A\to\Phi(A)
under
\Phi
-weighted colimits, and let
T
be a
\Phi
-cocontinuous monad on
\Phi(A)
. Since
T
is
\Phi
-cocontinuous, it preserves
(A\to\Phi(A))
-absolute colimits
[
Kel82
, Theorems 5.29 & 5.35]
. Hence, the forgetful functor
u_{T}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T)\to\Phi(A)
strictly creates
(A\to\Phi(A))
-absolute colimits (cf.
[
Bor94
, Proposition 4.3.2]
). Consequently, since every cocompletion is dense, and
u_{T}
admits a left
(A\to\Phi(A))
-adjoint
[
AM24
, Proposition 5.29]
,
Theorem

5.2
implies that the forgetful functor
u_{T}
is strictly
(A\to\Phi(A))
-monadic. For instance, the category of algebras for a finitary monad
T
on a locally finitely presentable category
E
is the category of algebras for the
(E_{\mathrm{fp}}\hookrightarrow E)
-monad induced by precomposing
T
with the inclusion of the full subcategory
E_{\mathrm{fp}}
of finitely presentable objects in
E

[
AM24
, Proposition 5.36]
.

Example

5.9
gives an alternative method to
Example

5.6
for proving that finitary algebraic theories induce
({\mathbb{F}}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{Set}})
-relative monads, at least supposing that one already knows that every algebraic theory induces a sifted-cocontinuous monad on
{\mathbf{Set}}
(which is the cocompletion of
{\mathbb{F}}
under sifted colimits).

In the third situation, one has a presentation of a structure by operations and equations, and consequently an induced notion of algebra for the presentation. For instance, we may show that the category of algebras for any quantitative equational theory in the sense of
[
MPP16
, Definition 2.2]
is relatively monadic. We give the specific example of quantitative semigroups below; the general case follows analogously.

Example 5.10
.

Denote by
\mathbf{Met}
the category of extended metric spaces and nonexpanding maps, and by
j\colon\mathbf{FinMet}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{Met}
the full subcategory inclusion of the finite metric spaces. For a metric space
X
, denote by
d_{X}\colon X\times X\to[0,\infty]
its distance function. Since
\mathbf{Met}
is a cartesian-monoidal category, we may consider the category
\mathbf{Semigrp}(\mathbf{Met})
of semigroups internal to
\mathbf{Met}
, i.e. metric spaces
X
equipped with an associative function
{({-})}\star{({-})}\colon X\times X\to X
such that
\max\{d_{X}(x_{1},x_{1}^{\prime}),d_{X}(x_{2},x_{2}^{\prime})\}\geq d_{X}((x_{1}\star x_{2}),(x_{1}^{\prime}\star x_{2}^{\prime}))
.
The forgetful functor
u\colon\mathbf{Semigrp}(\mathbf{Met})\to\mathbf{Met}
admits a left adjoint (an explicit construction is given in
[
MPP16
, §6]
), and hence a left
j
-adjoint
[
AM24
, Proposition 5.29]
.

Moreover, we may prove that
u
strictly creates every
j
-absolute colimit
C\mathrel{:=}\operatorname{colim}_{i}(u(D_{i}))
, where
D
is a diagram in
\mathbf{Semigrp}(\mathbf{Met})
.
To do so, we shall show that each such
C
admits a unique semigroup structure such that the coprojections
\text{\rotatebox[origin]{-180.0}{$\pi$}}_{i}
are semigroup homomorphisms.
Since the nerve of
j
preserves the colimit
C
by assumption, every nonexpansive map
X\to C
with finite domain factors through some coprojection
\text{\rotatebox[origin]{-180.0}{$\pi$}}_{i}\colon D_{i}\to C
.
In particular, every finite subobject of
C
factors thus, and consequently every finite subset of
C
is equal to the image
\text{\rotatebox[origin]{-180.0}{$\pi$}}_{i}(S)
, for some
i\in|D|
, of a subset
S\subseteq D_{i}
, such that
d_{D_{i}}(x,x^{\prime})=d_{C}(\text{\rotatebox[origin]{-180.0}{$\pi$}}_{i}(x),\text{\rotatebox[origin]{-180.0}{$\pi$}}_{i}(x^{\prime}))
for each pair
x,x^{\prime}\in S
.
Uniqueness of the binary operation
\star
on
C
follows by considering two-element subsets, and associativity by considering three-element subsets.
Nonexpansiveness of
\star
follows by considering a four-element subset, and using the condition on
d_{D_{i}}
above.

It thereby follows that
u
is strictly
(\mathbf{FinMet}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{Met})
-monadic.

Example

5.10
gives another alternative method to
Example

5.6
, since every finitary algebraic theory admits a presentation
[
Bir35
]
.
In fact, the three situations we have described – theories, cocontinuous monads, and presentations – are all facets of a more general relationship. To illustrate this, we give one final example: the relative monadicity of categories of algebras for a
j
-theory in the sense of
[
Ark22
,
LP23
]
.

Example 5.11
.

Let
{\mathbb{V}}
be a locally small closed symmetric monoidal category with equalisers, embedding into a complete closed symmetric monoidal category
{\mathbb{V}}^{\prime}

[
Kel82
, §3.11 & §3.12]
. Let
j\colon A\to E
be a dense and fully faithful
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor, and let
\ell\colon A\to B
be a
j
-theory, i.e. an identity-on-objects
{\mathbb{V}}
-functor admitting a right
j
-adjoint
r\colon B\to E
. The category of
(concrete) algebras
for
\ell
is defined to be the following pullback in
{\mathbb{V}}^{\prime}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}

[
LP23
, Definition 3.3]
; we denote by
\!\text{\char 136\relax}\!_{B}
the Yoneda embedding.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell\textup{-}\mathbf{Alg}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[B{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbb{V}}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[A{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbb{V}}]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u_{\ell}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces n_{j}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces[\ell{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbb{V}}]}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\!\text{\char 136\relax}\!_{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\it{pb}}

Just as in
Example

5.6
, it follows that the pullback is equivalent to the pseudopullback, and that
u_{\ell}
strictly creates
j
-absolute colimits. The projection
{\mathbb{V}}^{\prime}
-functor
n\colon\ell\textup{-}\mathbf{Alg}\to[B{}^{\mathrm{op}},{\mathbb{V}}]
is fully faithful, since
j
is dense and fully faithful functors are closed under pullback. The relative adjunction
B(\ell,1)\cong E(j,r)
consequently induces a mediating
{\mathbb{V}}^{\prime}
-functor
i\colon B\to\ell\textup{-}\mathbf{Alg}
, which is fully faithful, since
i\mathbin{;}n\cong\!\text{\char 136\relax}\!_{B}
and
n
and
\!\text{\char 136\relax}\!_{B}
are fully faithful. By
[
Kel82
, Proposition 5.16]
, we therefore have
n\cong n_{i}
. Pseudocommutativity of the pseudopullback square thus asserts that
(\ell\mathbin{;}i)\colon A\to\ell\textup{-}\mathbf{Alg}
is left-
j
-adjoint to
u_{\ell}
.
Consequently, by
Theorem

5.2
, the category of algebras for
\ell
is strictly
j
-monadic in
{\mathbb{V}}^{\prime}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
. When
u_{\ell}
furthermore admits a left adjoint (i.e.
\ell
is
admissible
in the sense of
[
LP23
, Definition 3.12]
), it is strictly monadic in
{\mathbb{V}}^{\prime}\textup{-}{\mathbf{\mathbb{C}at}}
by
Proposition

4.12
, recovering
[
LP23
, Proposition 4.5]
.

Example

5.11
turns out to subsume the previous examples. However, explicating this connection is beyond the scope of the present paper. In future work, we shall develop this connection fully, establishing a formal correspondence between these notions (cf.
[
Ark22
,
Ark22a
,
LP23
,
LP22
]
).

6.
A pasting law for relatively monadic adjunctions

In this section, we recall the pasting law for relative adjunctions and show that it respects relative monadicity in an appropriate sense. As a consequence, we derive necessary and sufficient conditions for the composite
(r\mathbin{;}r^{\prime})
of a tight-cell
r
with a
j
-monadic tight-cell
r^{\prime}
to be
j
-monadic. We continue to work in the context of a virtual equipment
\mathbb{X}
.

Lemma 6.1

(
[
AM24
, Proposition 5.30]
)
.

Consider the following diagram.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

The left triangle is a relative adjunction (
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{\ell^{\prime}}}r
) if and only if the outer triangle is a relative adjunction (
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}r\mathbin{;}r^{\prime}
).

We shall specialise
Lemma

6.1
to the case in which
r^{\prime}
is strictly
j
-monadic, and study the algebras for the relative monads induced by the corresponding relative adjunctions.

Lemma 6.2
.

Consider the following situation, and let
T
be the
f_{T^{\prime}}
-monad induced by
\ell\mathrel{\dashv_{f_{T^{\prime}}}}r
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces E}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces j}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u_{T^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{T^{\prime}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ell}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

Postcomposition by
u_{T^{\prime}}
induces a bijection between
T
-algebras and
(T\mathbin{;}u_{T^{\prime}})
-algebras, and their graded morphisms.

Proof.

We denote the carrier of the
f_{T^{\prime}}
-monad
T
by
t=(\ell\mathbin{;}r)
, the unit by
\eta\colon f_{T^{\prime}}\Rightarrow t
, and the extension operator by
\dagger\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})(f_{T^{\prime}},t)\Rightarrow\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})(t,t)
;
and denote the transposition operators of the relative adjunction
f_{T^{\prime}}\mathrel{\dashv_{j}}u_{T^{\prime}}
by

\sharp^{\prime}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})(f_{T^{\prime}},1)\cong E(j,r)\penalty\mskip 6.0mu plus 1.0mu\mathpunct{}\nonscript\mkern-3.0mu{:}\mskip 2.0mu\flat^{\prime}
.
Recall that every
T
-algebra (morphism) induces a
(T\mathbin{;}u_{T^{\prime}})
-algebra (morphism) by postcomposing
u_{T^{\prime}}
(
[
AM24
, Proposition 6.27]
), and that every
(T\mathbin{;}u_{T^{\prime}})
-algebra (morphism) induces a
T^{\prime}
-algebra (morphism) via the left-morphism
(r,\eta)
.

Given a
(T\mathbin{;}u_{T^{\prime}})
-algebra
(e,{\rtimes}^{\prime})
, we shall construct a
T
-algebra. The carrier
x\colon X\to\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})
is induced by the universal property of
\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})
from the
T^{\prime}
-algebra induced by
(r,\eta)
. For the algebra structure, observe that the 2-cell
{\rtimes}^{\prime}\colon E(j,e)\Rightarrow E(u_{T^{\prime}}t,e)
forms an
(E(j,e))
-graded
T^{\prime}
-algebra morphism in the sense of
Remark

2.4
, from
(T\mathbin{;}u_{T^{\prime}})
to the induced
T^{\prime}
-algebra on
e
, following
[
AM24
, Example 6.31]
. Hence, the universal property of
\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})
induces a 2-cell
{\langle\rangle}_{{\rtimes}^{\prime}}\colon E(j,e)\Rightarrow\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})(t,x)
such that postcomposition by
u_{T^{\prime}}
yields
{\rtimes}^{\prime}
. Let
{\rtimes}
be as follows.

{\rtimes}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})(f_{T^{\prime}},x)\xRightarrow{\sharp^{\prime}(1,x)}E(j,u_{T^{\prime}}x)=E(j,e)\xRightarrow{{\langle\rangle}_{{\rtimes}^{\prime}}}\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})(t,x)

The pair
(x,{\rtimes})
forms a
T
-algebra. The unit law follows: (
1.1
) by the
\sharp^{\prime}
–
\flat^{\prime}
isomorphism; (
1.2
) by bending
u_{T^{\prime}}
; (
1.3
) by the definition of
{\langle\rangle}_{{\rtimes}^{\prime}}
; (
1.4
) by the unit law for
{\rtimes}^{\prime}
; and (
1.5
) by the
\sharp^{\prime}
–
\flat^{\prime}
isomorphism. To show the extension law, it suffices to show the equality of the corresponding 2-cells under postcomposition by
u_{T^{\prime}}
, using the universal property of
\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})
. This equality follows: (
2.1
) by the definition of
{\langle\rangle}_{{\rtimes}^{\prime}}
; (
2.2
) by the
\sharp^{\prime}
–
\flat^{\prime}
isomorphism; (
2.3
) by the extension operator law for
{\rtimes}^{\prime}
; and (
2.4
) by the definition of
{\langle\rangle}_{{\rtimes}^{\prime}}
twice.

Every
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})
-graded
(T\mathbin{;}u_{T^{\prime}})
-algebra morphism
\epsilon\colon(e_{1},{\rtimes}_{1}^{\prime})\to(e_{2},{\rtimes}_{2}^{\prime})
, is also a
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})
-graded
T^{\prime}
-algebra morphism between the induced
T^{\prime}
-algebras. By the universal property of
\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})
,
\epsilon
thus induces a 2-cell
{\langle\rangle}_{\epsilon}\colon\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})(1,x_{1}),p_{1},\ldots,p_{n}\Rightarrow\mathbf{Alg}(T^{\prime})(1,x_{2})
. This is a
(p_{1},\ldots,p_{n})
-graded
T
-algebra morphism
(x_{1},{\rtimes}_{1})\to(x_{2},{\rtimes}_{2})
since, by postcomposing
u_{T^{\prime}}
, we have:

We must now show that these assignments are inverse to one another. Suppose we have a
T
-algebra
(x,{\rtimes})
, inducing a
(T\mathbin{;}u_{T^{\prime}})
-algebra
((e\mathbin{;}u_{T^{\prime}}),{\rtimes}^{\prime})

T^{\prime}
-algebra induced by
x
coincides with that induced by the
(T\mathbin{;}u_{T^{\prime}})
-algebra. By definition
(x\mathbin{;}u_{T^{\prime}})
is the carrier of both

-algebras. Using the unit law for
{\rtimes}

T^{\prime}
